name: Correlation as causation
short: Two things go together, so one is said to cause the other.
text: An association alone cannot tell cause from chance, a shared cause or reverse causation. A causal claim needs a design or analysis that rules those out.
example: Matthews (2000): across 17 European countries, stork pairs correlated with birth rates (r ≈ 0.62, p = 0.008).

ref.cite: Hill (1965). The environment and disease: association or causation? Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine.

name: Hidden third factor
short: Something else drives both the supposed cause and the outcome.
text: A confounder causes both the exposure and the outcome, so the two move together even if one has no effect on the other.
example: HRT looked heart-protective in observational studies; the WHI trial (2002) found a higher coronary risk (HR 1.29).

ref.cite: Greenland, Pearl & Robins (1999). Causal diagrams for epidemiologic research. Epidemiology.

name: Reverse causation
short: The outcome may be causing the supposed cause.
text: When exposure and outcome are measured together, the arrow can point the other way: illness changes habits, poor results change policies.
example: Shaper et al. (1988): non-drinkers' higher death rates partly reflected ill men who had stopped drinking.

ref.cite: Sattar & Preiss (2017). Reverse causality in cardiovascular epidemiological research: more common than imagined? Circulation.

name: Two trends, one clock
short: Two series that both drift over time correlate, whatever links them.
text: Anything that rises or falls steadily over the years correlates with anything else that does. Compare year-on-year changes, not levels.
example: Yule (1926): Church of England marriages and mortality in England and Wales, 1866–1911, correlated at r = 0.95.

ref.cite: Yule (1926). Why do we sometimes get nonsense-correlations between time-series? Journal of the Royal Statistical Society.

name: Collider bias
short: Selecting on a shared consequence creates, hides or flips a link.
text: If only cases with a common effect are studied (hospital patients, published papers, low-weight babies), two unrelated causes of it appear linked.
example: Birth-weight paradox: among low-birth-weight babies, maternal smoking looked protective (Hernández-Díaz et al. 2006).

ref.cite: Berkson (1946). Limitations of the application of fourfold table analysis to hospital data. Biometrics Bulletin.

name: Immortal time
short: A group is defined by something later, so its members had to survive to join it.
text: Counting the time before someone becomes 'exposed' as exposed time gives that group a head start in survival it did not earn.
example: Oscar winners seemed to live 3.9 years longer; counted correctly, the gap was about 1 year and not significant (Sylvestre et al. 2006).

ref.cite: Suissa (2008). Immortal time bias in pharmacoepidemiology. American Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Beyond the data
short: A trend is stretched far past the range where it was observed.
text: A pattern seen over one range of doses, ages or years need not hold outside it. Straight lines rarely stay straight.
example: Tatem et al. (2004) extended Olympic 100 m trends to predict that women would outrun men in 2156.

ref.cite: Altman & Bland (1998). Generalisation and extrapolation. BMJ.

name: Mice to people
short: A result in cells, animals or simulations is claimed for people.
text: Models are where hypotheses start. Many effects found in cells or animals shrink, vanish or reverse in human trials.
example: TGN1412 (2006): a dose 1/500 of the level safe in monkeys gave all six volunteers a severe inflammatory reaction.

ref.cite: Perel et al. (2007). Comparison of treatment effects between animal experiments and clinical trials: systematic review. BMJ.

name: Ecological fallacy
short: A pattern across groups is read as true of the individuals in them.
text: Countries, regions or schools can show a correlation that runs the other way, or not at all, among the people inside them.
example: US 1930: states with more immigrants had less illiteracy (r ≈ −0.53), yet immigrants were slightly more often illiterate.

ref.cite: Robinson (1950). Ecological correlations and the behavior of individuals. American Sociological Review.

name: Survivorship bias
short: Only the cases that made it through are looked at.
text: Failed firms, closed funds, dropped-out patients and lost planes leave no data. Studying the survivors shows what survival looks like, not what causes it.
example: WWII: Wald used damage on returning bombers to estimate vulnerability; places rarely hit on survivors were likely the deadliest.

ref.cite: Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross (1992). Survivorship bias in performance studies. Review of Financial Studies.

name: Unrepresentative sample
short: The people who answered differ from the people the claim is about.
text: A huge sample does not fix a skewed one. Volunteers, online panels and readers of one magazine are not the population.
example: Literary Digest, 1936: about 2.4 million returned ballots predicted Landon; Roosevelt won in a landslide.

ref.cite: Squire (1988). Why the 1936 Literary Digest poll failed. Public Opinion Quarterly.

name: Narrow sample, universal claim
short: One kind of participant, a claim about all humans.
text: Results from students, one country or one culture are written up as facts about people in general.
example: Henrich et al. (2010): 96% of psychology samples came from countries with 12% of the world's population.

ref.cite: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

name: Simpson's paradox
short: A trend in the pooled data reverses or vanishes within subgroups.
text: When groups differ in size and baseline, adding them together can flip a comparison. The right level depends on the causal question.
example: Berkeley, 1973: 44% of men vs 35% of women admitted; by department, little bias, if anything favouring women.

ref.cite: Simpson (1951). The interpretation of interaction in contingency tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B.

name: Regression to the mean
short: Extreme values drift back toward average on their own.
text: Anything picked because it was unusually high or low tends to be less extreme next time, with or without the treatment.
example: Galton (1886): children of very tall or very short parents were, on average, closer to the mean height.

ref.cite: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson (2004). Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it. International Journal of Epidemiology.

name: Small numbers, wild swings
short: Small groups give extreme results by chance, at both ends.
text: The fewer the cases, the more a rate jumps around. The best and the worst of a league table are often just the smallest.
example: Wainer (2007): US counties with the lowest kidney-cancer rates were mostly small and rural, and so were the highest.

ref.cite: Tversky & Kahneman (1971). Belief in the law of small numbers. Psychological Bulletin.

name: Base-rate neglect
short: How rare the condition is gets ignored.
text: When something is rare, even an accurate test or detector produces mostly false alarms. The base rate decides what a positive result means.
example: Casscells et al. (1978): the commonest answer from 60 Harvard doctors and students was 95%; the right one is about 2%.

ref.cite: Bar-Hillel (1980). The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments. Acta Psychologica.

name: Transposed conditional
short: The chance of the data given a hypothesis is read as the chance of the hypothesis.
text: P(evidence | innocent) is not P(innocent | evidence), and p = 0.01 is not a 1% chance that the effect is a fluke.
example: Sally Clark trial: press reported '1 in 73 million' as the chance the two deaths were accidental (RSS, 2002).

ref.cite: Thompson & Schumann (1987). Interpretation of statistical evidence in criminal trials: the prosecutor's fallacy and the defense attorney's fallacy. Law and Human Behavior.

name: No significance, no effect
short: A non-significant result is reported as proof of no effect.
text: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. A wide confidence interval that includes zero can also include effects worth caring about.
example: Amrhein et al. (2019): a risk ratio of 1.2 with P = 0.091 was reported as 'no association'.

ref.cite: Altman & Bland (1995). Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ.

name: Significant but trivial
short: A tiny effect is sold as important because p is small.
text: With a big enough sample, almost any difference is 'significant'. Statistical significance says nothing about size or importance.
example: Kramer et al. (2014): with 689,003 Facebook users, effects as small as d = 0.001 were statistically significant.

ref.cite: Sullivan & Feinn (2012). Using effect size, or why the P value is not enough. Journal of Graduate Medical Education.

name: Relative risk alone
short: 'Doubles the risk' without saying risk of what, from how much.
text: A 100% rise from 1 in 7,000 is 1 extra case in 7,000. Without the absolute numbers, a relative change can't be judged.
example: UK 1995: a warning that newer pills doubled clot risk (about 1 to 2 in 7,000) was followed by some 13,000 extra abortions.

ref.cite: Gigerenzer et al. (2007). Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.

name: Distorted chart
short: The picture exaggerates what the numbers say.
text: A cut-off axis, two different scales or a stretched time window can make a small change look dramatic, or a big one vanish.
example: A 2015 US House hearing chart used two unlabelled scales, so ~327,000 abortions seemed to overtake ~935,000 cancer screenings.

ref.cite: Pandey et al. (2015). How deceptive are deceptive visualizations? An empirical analysis of common distortion techniques. CHI '15.

name: Overfitting
short: A model fits the past closely and predicts the future badly.
text: Many predictors and few cases let a model learn the noise. Only performance on new data shows what it really knows.
example: Google Flu Trends overestimated flu in 100 of 108 weeks from August 2011, more than double in February 2013 (Lazer et al. 2014).

ref.cite: Babyak (2004). What you see may not be what you get: a brief, nontechnical introduction to overfitting in regression-type models. Psychosomatic Medicine.

name: Forking paths
short: The analysis was chosen after seeing the data.
text: Trying other outcomes, covariates, exclusions or stopping points until p < 0.05 makes false positives likely, even without bad intent.
example: Simmons et al. (2011): flexible analysis 'showed' that hearing a Beatles song made people nearly 18 months younger.

ref.cite: Gelman & Loken (2014). The statistical crisis in science. American Scientist.

name: Many tests, one hit
short: Out of many comparisons, the one that came up significant is reported.
text: Test 20 true nulls at p < 0.05 and expect one hit. Without correction, a lone significant result among many is likely noise.
example: Bennett et al. (2009): uncorrected fMRI tests found 'active' voxels in a dead salmon shown photos of people.

ref.cite: Bender & Lange (2001). Adjusting for multiple testing: when and how? Journal of Clinical Epidemiology.

name: Subgroup surprise
short: The effect is claimed for one subgroup found after the fact.
text: Slice a trial enough ways and some slice will differ by chance. Credible subgroup effects are few, prespecified and tested as interactions.
example: ISIS-2 (1988): aspirin helped after heart attack, except, apparently, in patients born under Gemini or Libra.

ref.cite: Sun, Briel, Walter & Guyatt (2010). Is a subgroup effect believable? Updating criteria to evaluate the credibility of subgroup analyses. BMJ.

name: File drawer
short: The published studies are the ones that worked.
text: Null results stay unpublished, so the literature, and any review of it, overstates the effect.
example: Turner et al. (2008): 94% of published antidepressant trials looked positive; by FDA review, 51% were.

ref.cite: Rosenthal (1979). The file drawer problem and tolerance for null results. Psychological Bulletin.

name: One study, settled
short: One striking study is treated as established fact.
text: A first result, especially a small and surprising one, is a lead to follow up. Many fail to replicate.
example: Power posing (2010, 42 people) reported hormone changes; a 200-person replication found none (Ranehill et al. 2015).

ref.cite: Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science.

name: Surrogate endpoint
short: A marker improved, so people are assumed to be better off.
text: Blood values, test scores and clicks stand in for what matters. Changing the marker need not change the outcome, and can worsen it.
example: CAST (1991): drugs suppressed irregular heartbeats, yet 63 patients died on drug vs 26 on placebo.

ref.cite: Fleming & DeMets (1996). Surrogate end points in clinical trials: are we being misled? Annals of Internal Medicine.

name: Survival-time illusion
short: Earlier diagnosis can lengthen survival without delaying death.
text: Screening starts the clock sooner and finds harmless cases, so survival after diagnosis rises even if no one lives longer. Look at mortality.
example: South Korea: screening raised thyroid-cancer diagnoses 15-fold by 2011 while deaths stayed flat (Ahn et al. 2014).

ref.cite: Welch, Schwartz & Woloshin (2000). Are increasing 5-year survival rates evidence of success against cancer? JAMA.

name: Changed yardstick
short: The count rose because the definition or the counting changed.
text: New criteria, more testing or better reporting can create a rise or fall in the numbers with no change in the world.
example: Denmark: about 60% of the rise in autism diagnoses was explained by changed criteria and reporting (Hansen et al. 2015).

ref.cite: Hansen, Schendel & Parner (2015). Explaining the increase in the prevalence of autism spectrum disorders. JAMA Pediatrics.
